Three years reigned he--</hi>(compare <reference osisRef="1Kgs.15.1">1Ki 15:1</reference> with <reference osisRef="1Kgs.15.9">1Ki 15:9</reference>). Parts of years are often counted in Scripture as whole years. The reign began in Jeroboam's eighteenth year, continued till the nineteenth, and ended in the course of the twentieth.<div eID="gen4541" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4542" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">his mother's name was Maachah--</hi>or Michaiah (<reference osisRef="2Chr.13.2">2Ch 13:2</reference>), probably altered from the one to the other on her becoming queen, as was very common under a change of circumstances. She is called the daughter of Abishalom, or Absalom (<reference osisRef="2Chr.11.21">2Ch 11:21</reference>), of Uriel (<reference osisRef="2Chr.13.2">2Ch 13:2</reference>). Hence, it has been thought probable that Tamar, the daughter of Absalom (<reference osisRef="2Sam.14.27">2Sa 14:27</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Sam.18.18">18:18</reference>), had been married to Uriel, and that Maachah was their daughter. <div eID="gen4542" type="x-p"/>

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv3246"/><div sID="gen4543" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv3246"/><hi type="bold">3. his heart was not perfect with the Lord ... , as the heart of David his father--</hi>(Compare <reference osisRef="1Kgs.11.4">1Ki 11:4</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Kgs.14.22">14:22</reference>). He was not positively bad at first, for it appears that he had done something to restore the pillaged treasures of the temple (<reference osisRef="1Kgs.15.15">1Ki 15:15</reference>). This phrase contains a comparative reference to David's heart. His doing that which was right in the eyes of the Lord (<reference osisRef="1Kgs.15.5">1Ki 15:5</reference>) is frequently used in speaking of the kings of Judah, and means only that they did or did not do that which, in the general course and tendency of their government, was acceptable to God. It furnishes no evidence as to the lawfulness or piety of one specific act. <div eID="gen4543" type="x-p"/>

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv3251"/><div sID="gen4551" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv3251"/><hi type="bold">16-17. there was war between Asa and Baasha king of Israel all their days--</hi>Asa enjoyed a ten years' peace after Jeroboam's defeat by Abijam, and this interval was wisely and energetically spent in making internal reforms, as well as increasing the means of national defense (<reference osisRef="2Chr.14.1-2Chr.14.7">2Ch 14:1-7</reference>). In the fifteenth year of his reign, however, the king of Israel commenced hostilities against him, and, invading his kingdom, erected a strong fortress at Ramah, which was near Gibeah, and only six Roman miles from Jerusalem. Afraid lest his subjects might quit his kingdom and return to the worship of their fathers, he wished to cut off all intercourse between the two nations. Ramah stood on an eminence overhanging a narrow ravine which separated Israel from Judah, and therefore he took up a hostile position in that place. <div eID="gen4551" type="x-p"/>

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv3252"/><div sID="gen4552" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv3252"/><hi type="bold">18-20. Then Asa took all the silver and the gold that were left in the ... house of the Lord--</hi>Asa's religious character is now seen to decline. He trusted not in the Lord (<reference osisRef="2Chr.16.7">2Ch 16:7</reference>). In this emergency Asa solicited the powerful aid of the king of Damascene-Syria; and to bribe him to break off his alliance with Baasha, he transmitted to him the treasure lying in the temple and palace. The Syrian mercenaries were gained. Instances are to be found, both in the ancient and modern history of the East, of the violation of treaties equally sudden and unscrupulous, through the presentation of some tempting bribe. Ben-hadad poured an army into the northern provinces of Israel, and having captured some cities in Galilee, on the borders of Syria, compelled Baasha to withdraw from Ramah back within his own territories.<div eID="gen4552" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4553" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Ben-hadad--</hi>(See on <reference osisRef="1Kgs.11.14">1Ki 11:14</reference>). <div eID="gen4553" type="x-p"/>
